courses.actualProfile: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives

It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.

courses.actualProfile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
courses.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.

In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.

courses.actualProfile: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3

courses.actualProfile: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.
courses.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.

courses.actualProfile: This course offers a broad approach to human rights: the legal, the historical and the theoretical/philosophical. In the first part of the course, human rights will mainly be studied in a legal way, adopting a legal perspective. Students will be introduced to the catalogue of human rights as positive law. Human rights treaties, the monitoring mechanisms and case law on human rights will be explored. This knowledge will be tested in a mid-term exam (multiple choice). In the second part, students will delve into a more historical and philosophical understanding of human rights. We will investigate the rise of the language of human rights in the 17th and 18th century, its culmination in the US Bill of Rights (1791) and the Déclaration des Droits de l’Homme et du Citoyen (1789). We will explore the further developments of the language in the 20th century in particular, which brought a great extension of the number and application of human rights. Students will read landmark cases that touch upon contentious, and often politicised disputes between liberty and equality. Some emphasis in this course will be given to natural law and its connection to human rights. We will delve into the classical and medieval scholarship on natural law, starting with Plato’s and Aquinas’ views on right and wrong. This will be compared to the modern views on the same going back to Hobbes and Locke, the latter considered to be the founding father of the rights paradigm. Human rights in today’s traditional societies will be investigated through selected case studies.
courses.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
courses.topics: human rights; french declaration; rights treaties; modern philosophers; traces; classical

courses.actualProfile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
courses.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.

courses.actualProfile: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.
courses.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
courses.topics: decline of political parties; impact of globalization; non majoritarian institutions; phenomena like democratic; like democratic backsliding; compare political systems

courses.actualProfile: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
courses.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

courses.actualProfile: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.
courses.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.

courses.actualProfile: Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_ But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?

courses.actualProfile: Functional Anatomy examines the structure of the human body in direct relation to function. In this course, anatomical structures and their functions are systematically studied together, at the level of body systems as well as individual anatomical components. The course is organised in thematic blocks, each addressing a specific anatomical region or system (the Skeletal System & Vertebral Column; Bony Thorax & Pelvis; Respiratory & Cardiovascular Systems; Abdomen; Reproductive & Lower Urinary Systems) and each emphasising specific anatomical and functional reasoning (rather than exhaustive memorisation). Within these blocks, learning activities are purposefully selected to support the intended learning outcomes, combining visual, spatial and experiential approaches. Anatomical understanding is developed through surface anatomy, medical imaging, scientific anatomical drawing and video-based human remain based material, complemented by carefully framed encounters with human skeletal remains, a dissection facility and in class clinical demonstrations. Together, these activities foster three-dimensional anatomical insight, spatial reasoning and awareness of anatomical variation. Please note that these are explicitly framed as academic learning experiences rather than clinical skills training. Studying human anatomy inevitably confronts students with an ethical paradox: respect for the human body is taught through its objectification for scientific study.
courses.description2: Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.

courses.actualProfile: Pharmacology is the science of drugs including their origin, composition, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity (Merriam-Webster Learner’s Dictionary). The functioning of the (diseased) human body can be affected by (medicinal) drugs, which act through a variety of molecular mechanisms. In this course, the basic principles of pharmacology will be discussed, followed by studies of different aspects of drugs and the human body to illustrate the se pharmacological principles which are used for rational drug develo pment and physiological use. The importance of neuronal, hormonal, immunological (whole body) and biochemical (whole cell) regulation for proper physiological and cellular function, and dysregulation during pathological processes are emphasized. Identification of potential drug t argets and the interaction of drugs with macromolecules (enzymes, cell surface receptors, and signaling molecules) as the main pharmacological principles are central in this course. Quantitative pharmacological, pharmacokinetic and statistical methods are used. At the end of the course you will be able to explain effectiv ely existing drug therapies in a rational way in terms of molecular targets, cellular actions and physiological consequences of pharmacological treatment. They will be able to suggest targets for drug development on the basis of pathophysiological insights a nd to apply pharmacological models when describing concentration-response, time-concentration, and time-response relationships of drugs.
courses.description2: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.

courses.actualProfile: Infectious diseases and disorders of the immune system are a continuous threat to the life and well-being of humans, animals and plants. Studying the fundamental processes in immunology, such as the recognition of self and non-self (e.g. microbes), development of mature lymphocyte receptor repertoires, and the innate and adaptive immune response is crucial for the understanding how the immune system deals with the daily threat of microorganisms. On the other hand, general knowledge of the highly diverse mic robial world is needed. From this knowledge, detailed specific understanding of microbial strategies to circumvent host resistance can be acquired. As a principle, the course will focus on interactions between host and infectious agents. Basic principles a s microbial virulence, inflammatory responses, tissue damage and apoptosis are discussed. In addition to normal immune responses to infectious agents, the course will also deal with immunopathological processes and diseases.
courses.description2: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.

courses.actualProfile: In this course the relation between the normal function (physiology) and disease (pathophysiology) is illustrated for six basal organ systems: 1. cardiovascular, 2. lung (pulmonology), 3. kidney (nephrology), 4. digestive tract, 5. endocrine glands (endocrinology) and 6. central nervous system. The aim of this course is to provide insight in the principles of the mechanisms of diseases. For the organ systems mentioned the student first has to study the embryology and anatomy, Using this information as starting point, the basic physiology is studied and using the combined knowledge the student must be able to derive the symptoms and failures in the system or the pathophysiology.
courses.description2: Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.

courses.actualProfile: Have you ever wondered what makes life on earth possible? The foundation of life, health & biomedical science course takes you on a journey into the building blocks of life, exploring how cells, molecules, and systems interact to create and sustain living organisms. Cells are at the heart of this story: they are the basic units of life, taking in energy and nutrients from their environment and converting them into biologically useful forms. Inside every cell lies genetic information, dna, that not only directs all cellular activities but also passes traits from one generation to the next. Mutations, recombination and epigenetics create variation, and this diversity fuels the evolutionary process through natural selection. The course is structured in four interconnected units: The cell as a unit of life Basic molecular biology Cellular physiology and communication Capita selecta (a series of explorations that give you a first taste of the diverse academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.) You will also work on a special research presentation assignment, which allows you to engage with scientific literature, reflect on how we know what we know, and experience how new knowledge can be generated. But this course is more than just an introduction. As a gateway course, foundation of life, health & biomedical science opens the door to exciting academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.
courses.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.

courses.actualProfile: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. courses.actualProfile: New discoveries and advancements in scientific research are proposed every day, all around us. It can be overwhelming to keep up. This course provides the foundation for students to understand a vast array of practical applications in a multitude of life science topics (e.g. industry, medicine, agriculture, ecology, etc.). Students w ill take a closer look at the cellular biology of mostly eukaryotes, but also prokaryotes, gaining a comprehensive understanding of cell structure and physio logy. Concepts from the LIFE101 course, Introduction to Life Sciences, will be revisited and students will dive deeper into the details of life processes to understand the underlying molecular mechanisms. Students will also learn to examine current research topics and methods used to study the invisible world of molecular biology. Students will be encouraged to question the reproducibility of results and to propose how modernization of existing methods (and/or theoretical) technologies would improve the limitations of research and the validity of results. The course consists of five themes: 1 – The fundamental units of life: Cellular components, chemistry and energetics 2 – Genomes: DNA to Proteins, replication, repair and regulation of gene expression 3 – Cellular dynamics: Membrane trafficking, transport and signaling pathways 4 – Cell fate: Cell division, tissues, stem cells and cancer 5 – Drug Mechanisms (Paper and Poster Project)

courses.actualProfile: Physiology is the study of the normal functioning of a living organism and its component parts, including all its chemical and physical processes. In this course, the focus is on the function of the adult human body and of different organ systems. Knowledge of the subject is essential for students with a medical interest and recommended for every student interested in the function (s) of the (own) human body. The course includes fundamental concepts of molecules, cellular and systems physiology to understand how the human body functions and maintains a steady state. Although some medical examples are used to illustrate general physiological principles, this is not a course in medical physiology. Still, the core of physiological knowledge you will learn by ta king Human Physiology will help you better understand human health and disease. The course will be divided in 4 units: (1) Basic cell processes , (2) Homeostasis and control, (3) Integration of function , and (4) Metabolism, growth, and aging . In addition there will be one individual assignment. Contents of the 4 course units are structure-function relationships (organelles, cells, tissues, organs), energy handling, homeostasis and control systems, signaling and communication, study of individual organ systems (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine, muscles, nervous, digestive, reproduction), and integration of functions.
courses.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.

courses.actualProfile: Living organisms evolved from the prebiotic world through chemical reactions. Laws governing those early reactions are the same t oday. C hemistry is the underlying science behind biology. Biochemistry, the chemistry of life, deals with the reactions that produce the molecules of life: proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids that enable the self -assembly and reproduction of simple and complex organisms. Although organisms vary en ormously in complexity and biological properties, all domains of life use similar biomolecules for encoding and transmitting information, intra - and intercellular signaling, formation of membranes, building and degrading macromolecules, energy metabolism, and many more features. Errors in the production, proper localization or degradation of these molecules can often lead to disease. Biochemical knowledge is not only essential for understanding and treating these diseases, but also necessary for advancing many applications in biotechnology.
courses.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.

courses.actualProfile: This course is designed for a broad group of UCR students interested in life sciences. This course provides an introduction to the biochemical and molecular laboratory work performed in most labs today, and hence is a highly recommended course for all life science and medical track students. The students will be introduced to the following themes: • Blood • Bacteria, handling hygiene and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) • Protein production, isolation and analysis • DNA isolation and analysis (digestion, PCR and gel electrophoresis) • Bioinformatics These themes are characteristic or representative of basic biological and clinical research. Additional clinical diagnostic themes are added whenever there is an opportunity. The concepts, principles and techniques used in this course regarding blood and blood proteins include a basic blood cell analysis (hemogram), protein electrophoresis, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and a patient case. Course outline HCBLIFE214; Life Science Laboratory Page 2 of 8 With respect to bacteria, students will first learn the skills for properly handling pure cultures. A series of tests will also be carried out to check hygiene and sterilization procedures, bacterial species determination and the effect of antibiotics on bacterial growth. It also includes genetic modification of bacteria using safe microbiological techniques. After students have become acquainted with the safe handling of bacteria, they will generate a genetically modified organism (GMO).

courses.methods: Laboratory methods; Experimental procedures; Data analysis

courses.actualProfile: This course covers a vast number of topics from general and molecular pathology and genetics of humans. The pathology portion includes the bases of pathology which is cell injury and cell death. The pathology also covers how acute and chronic inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis, and neoplasia contribute to pathologies. The course then shifts to understanding the molecular genetics underlying disease. The significance of chromosome structure and organization of genes will be covered along with gene mutations (and their inheritance) through several examples of genetic diseases. The course also focuses on the status of genetic testing and genetic treatments. Ethical and legal considerations for now and in the future will also be examined.
courses.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.

courses.actualProfile: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.

It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.

courses.actualProfile: The definition of what is a mental disorder is very complex, and there is no universal agreement about it. This course explores mental health and mental disorders across the lifespan, emphasizing a bio-psycho-social perspective that considers how biological, psychological, and social factors interact to promote mental health or contribute to the development of disorders. Students are introduced to historical and contemporary views of psychopathology, the prevalence and development of mental disorders, and the role of culture, gender, and environmental factors in shaping mental health and illness. The course familiarizes students with key concepts, terminology, theories, and research methods in psychopathology, while fostering critical thinking and analytical skills for evaluating mental health information. It addresses the assessment, diagnosis, classification, and treatment of mental disorders, including the most prevalent disorders from infancy through adulthood. Through interactive lectures, audiovisual materials, discussions, exercises, and written assignments, students gain a research-oriented understanding of maladaptive behavior and develop greater awareness of both their own mental health and the mental health of others within a comprehensive bio-psycho-social framework.
courses.description2: Provides a deep dive into factors shaping mental health. Teaches critical thinking, explores the bio‑psycho‑social approach and covers mental disorders, research findings and assessment techniques.

courses.actualProfile: In th is course, Medical and Health Psychology , we will examine the complex interplay between biological, psychological, and socio-cultural factors that influence health and illness. Guided by the core principle of the field, the bio-psycho-social approach of the human being, we will explore key theories, research findings, and specific interventions within clinical health psychology, with a particular focus on the role of psychological expertise and mental health professionals in medical settings. Based on the World Health Organization’s (1948) definition of Health as a state of physical, mental and social well-being with a special emphasis in the balance between these aspects , Health Psychology is concerned with the elements that influence health and illness across the individual lifespan. It considers the implication of multiple aspects that can be combined in a complex way to promote and maintain health or to contribute for the settlement of dysfunction or illness. Therefore, This course will provide stude nts with a comprehensive understanding of these determinants and factors by addressing the following core areas: 1) Attitudes, behavior and lifestyle factors affecting health and disease; 2) Stress and the related psychosocial factors and processes associated with disease development and progression; Course outline HCBPSYC311 Medical & Health Psychology Page 2 of 11 3) Biopsychosocial factors involved in the illness experience; as well as, the long -term social and psychological implications of chronic illness; 4) Relevance of psychological interventions in medical…

Therefore, this course will address the following subject ar¬eas: Contemporary views in Clinical Psychology, including psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies; 1. Ethical issues in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies; 2. Mental Health intervention processes: Psychodiagnostics and psychotherapies; 3. Clinical psychological assessment: Psychodiagnostics; 4. courses.actualProfile: How do we become unique individuals? Which factors influence this process and how do they interplay in each stage of our development during our lives? In this course we will explore these and many other questions about human development, where students will acquire knowledge and develop critical thinking and understanding of the main aspects related to human development throughout the lifespan. The main goal of the course Developmental Psychology is to introduce the student to the basic concepts, issues and me thods in the field, which is concerned with human physical, cognitive, social and emotional development throughout the lifespan: from pregnancy to infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and older age; their descriptions and understandings, as well as t he most relevant theoretical approaches and some psychological assessment and interventions in the different phases of life. Therefore, this course will address the following subject areas: 1. Historical and contemporary views, and main theories in Developmental Psychology; 2. Biological and environmental foundations of human development; 3. Pre-natal development and birth; 4. Attachment and physical, cognitive, emotional and social development in infancy. 5. Physical, cognitive, social, emotional and personality development in early and middle childhood, adolescence and early, middle and late adulthood; 6. End of life: death, dying, and bereavement.
courses.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.

courses.actualProfile: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. courses.actualProfile: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed.
courses.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
courses.topics: primary school children; local primary school; persuasive speaking; rhetorical theory; voices; public-speaking

courses.actualProfile: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.
courses.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
courses.topics: persuasion; framing; nudging; cognitive shortcuts; ethics of persuasion; climate communication
courses.finding: Persuasion/sustainability communication, not specialist oral-health messaging.
